questions.q: What kind of lock does a plain SELECT take under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level?
questions.explain: Ordinary reads take shared locks, which are compatible with other shared locks.

questions.q: Why can two different sessions both hold a shared lock on the same row at the same time?
options: Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, and reading doesn't change data so there's nothing for two readers to corrupt
SQL Server only allows one shared lock at a time, but silently queues the second
Shared locks only apply to the first session that requests them
Shared locks are actually the same thing as exclusive locks
questions.explain: Shared locks are mutually compatible, so any number of readers can hold one on the same resource simultaneously.

questions.q: What kind of lock does a shared lock conflict with?
options: Nothing — shared locks never conflict with anything
questions.explain: Shared locks are incompatible with exclusive locks, which is why a writer blocks a reader (and vice versa) on the same row.

questions.q: Under READ COMMITTED, when is a shared lock on a row released?
options: As soon as the read of that row finishes, even if the surrounding transaction is still open
Only when the entire transaction commits or rolls back
Never — shared locks are held permanently once taken
Only when the server is restarted
questions.explain: READ COMMITTED releases shared locks immediately after the read, unlike exclusive locks, which are held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.q: In sys.dm_tran_locks, what value in the request_mode column indicates a shared lock?
questions.explain: request_mode shows S for shared, X for exclusive, U for update, and Sch-M for schema modification locks.
